body:
VERIFIED against the code — and this is my own line from #1724, so worth stating
plainly rather than defending.

`cps/kobo.py`:

    request_lm = parse_kobo_timestamp(lm_str) or datetime.now(timezone.utc)

`request_lm` is not only mirrored back in the response to suppress the device's
conflict popup — it is ASSIGNED to `current_bookmark.last_modified`,
`statistics.last_modified`, `book_read.last_modified` and the parent reading
state. So an unparseable device clock is silently replaced by the server's wall
clock and stored as if the device had supplied it.

Consequence: a stale device's state can be recorded as newer than another
device's genuinely later timestamp, which is exactly the input later conflict
resolution trusts.

The docstring nearby says the field exists "only to mirror" the device's value,
which is how the fallback looked harmless. Mirroring is one of its jobs; being
the stored ordering clock is the other.

#1724 fixed the parse (a millisecond timestamp used to 400 the whole sync) and
deliberately made the parser non-throwing. The fallback for a value that STILL
does not parse was not revisited: a malformed clock should probably leave the
stored clock alone, or mark it unknown, rather than invent one.

---

UPDATE 2026-08-20 — reachability WIDENED by PR #1776, disclosed rather than left to be found.

#1776 fixes F-947bb8: `astimezone()` raises OverflowError (not ValueError) and sat OUTSIDE the
`try` in `parse_kobo_timestamp`, so an out-of-range `LastModified` used to escape the handler
entirely. The enclosing `except` at `cps/kobo.py:1774` catches
`(KeyError, TypeError, ValueError, StatementError)` — NOT OverflowError — so the reading-state PUT
failed and the device's position was not stored at all.

After #1776 the parser returns None for those values, which falls into

    request_lm = parse_kobo_timestamp(lm_str) or datetime.now(timezone.utc)

i.e. straight into THIS finding. So an input class that previously failed loudly now silently
invents a clock.

That is still net-better (a saved position with a wrong ordering clock beats a lost one) and it makes
an out-of-range clock behave identically to a malformed one, which always took this path because
`parse_kobo_timestamp` has always swallowed ValueError internally. But it means this finding now
covers TWO input classes instead of one, and the fix is worth more than it was.

Fix direction unchanged and still requires a decision: a clock we cannot trust should either leave
the stored clock alone or mark it unknown — never invent one. Deliberately not bundled into #1776,
because "do not throw" and "what should an untrusted clock do to stored state" are separate calls.
title: A malformed reading-state LastModified is stored as an invented server clock
